tagline: Cote d'Ivoire's western port and lagoon coast toward the Liberian frontier
summary: San-Pedro is Cote d'Ivoire's second-largest port and the commercial anchor of the country's western coast, the world's leading cocoa-export gateway set beside an Atlantic lagoon-and-beach coastline. West of Abidjan's dense lagoon system, San-Pedro frames a quieter coast of fishing communities, the resort-leaning beaches toward Sassandra, and lagoon inlets that fringe the shore toward the Liberian frontier. The open Atlantic here carries surf, but the port approaches and lagoon reaches offer sheltered water, and San-Pedro's role as a regional economic hub gives it business and coastal-community mobility demand. Today the coast has no organised passenger-vessel layer — movement between San-Pedro, its lagoon communities and the coastal towns is entirely road-bound.

transit_planning: Cote d'Ivoire's transport investment concentrates on the Abidjan lagoon network and the port corridors; the western coast around San-Pedro remains road-dependent with informal boats on the lagoons. A structured marine layer adds coastal and lagoon links along a stretch less served by roads than the Abidjan axis.

competitive_landscape: San-Pedro's western coast has no organised passenger-vessel operator; the lagoons are served by informal fishing craft and coastal movement is road-bound. As the country's second port and cocoa gateway, the business and community demand is real, and the less-developed western road network sharpens the case for a coastal water layer — a wholly open corridor.
seasonality: The Atlantic surf is a year-round factor, strongest in the May–July main rainy season; the sheltered lagoon reaches stay workable through the year while open-coast legs are swell-gated. The drier November–March window offers the calmest open-water conditions and peak leisure demand toward Sassandra.
regulatory_note: Cote d'Ivoire's maritime passenger operations fall under the national maritime authority; coastal and lagoon craft sit within domestic licensing, coordinated with the San-Pedro port authority for harbour approaches. Routing near the Liberian frontier stays clear of the border, favouring transparent, scheduled operations along the domestic coast.
